newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge upholds Mass. tobacco disclosure law.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge upholds Mass. tobacco disclosure law.

text.p: A federal judge on Friday upheld a Massachusetts law requiring tobacco companies to disclose the ingredients of their cigarette brands, saying the measure "is in harmony with the purpose Congress expressed."

Philip Morris Cos.Inc., R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., Brown and Williamson Tobacco Corp. and Lorillard Tobacco Co. had filed suit trying to block the disclosure of their brand's ingredients, saying they should not be required to reveal trade secrets.

The companies said they would apeal the judge's ruling upholding the law, which requires tobacco companies to disclose ingredients in specific brands by "weight, measure or numerical count" to the state Department of Public Health.

U.S. District Judge George O'Toole said in an 18-page ruling: "It might even be said that the Massachusetts statute is in harmony with the purpose Congress expressed when it adopted (a law) 'to provide a new strategy for making Americans more aware of any adverse health effects of smoking, to assure the timely and widespread dissemination of research findings and to enable individuals to make informed decisions about smoking."

"We obviously disagree with the ruling," said David Remes, a Washington-based lawyer acting as spokesman for the companies. "Just this Wednesday another federal court in Alabama held that a state could not disclose the same information that this ruling permits."
Massachusetts Assistant Attorney General Rebecca McIntyre said she expected the tobacco companies' action, saying, "This is what they do. They exhaust all avenues of appeal.
"We're going to oppose their efforts to have this case appealed ... and we're going to continue to go forward to implement the statute," she said.

The Massachusetts law, which goes into effect July 1, goes further than current federal statutes, which require the firms to disclose additional ingredients, without identifying the brand or particular maker, to the secretary of Health and Human Services and prohibits their disclosure to the public.
"Unlike the federal statute," O'Toole noted, "the Massachusetts act contemplates that, subject to some conditions, ingredient information will be made public."
Indeed, the state legislator who sponsored the law, Sen. Warren Tolman, D-Middlesex, said, "I fully expect the information will be available on the Internet."

O'Toole, however, found no conflict between the federal law and the state measure saying, "There is no danger that the (firms') reporting of cigarette ingredients to the Secretary will be disturbed by the enforcement of the Massachusetts statute...

"What may be disturbed is the (firms') ability to keep their ingredient information confidential. That is a legitimate concern for them," O'Toole conceded, but added, "there simply is no basis for concluding that it was Congress' purpose in enacting (the federal law) to grant general trade secret or confidentiality protection to the plaintiffs' ingredient information."
